entry.title: Why Arrays Are Faster Than Linked Lists (It Starts with the CPU Cache!)

link.title: Why Arrays Are Faster Than Linked Lists (It Starts with the CPU Cache!)

entry.content:
Most of us learn the classic computer science rule:

Array access → O(1) Linked list access → O(n)

But in real-world systems, Big-O notation doesn’t tell the whole story.

Performance is often dominated by something entirely different: the CPU cache. 🧠

Here is why your algorithm’s speed is dictated by hardware, not just math. 👇

1. The Bottleneck: RAM vs. CPU Cache

Modern CPUs are blazingly quick, but RAM is relatively slow. To avoid sitting idle waiting for RAM to deliver data, the CPU uses built-in cache memory:

  • L1 Cache → extremely fast, but very small
  • L2 Cache → medium speed and size
  • L3 Cache → larger, but slower

The Key Idea

The CPU doesn’t load memory byte-by-byte. It loads a “cache line” (usually a 64-byte block). If you ask for one value, the CPU grabs that value plus several neighboring values and pulls them all into the ultra-fast cache.

2. The Array Advantage: Spatial Locality

This is where arrays shine. Arrays are stored in continuous memory.

Index:  0    1    2    3    4
Array: [10] [20] [30] [40] [50]

When the CPU reads array[0], it doesn’t just get 10. It loads a whole cache line into L1: [10][20][30][40].

When your loop moves to array[1], the CPU doesn’t have to talk to the slow RAM at all. The data is already in the cache! This results in an extremely fast traversal known as “spatial locality.”

3. The Linked List Problem: Cache Misses

Linked list nodes are allocated dynamically, meaning they are stored randomly across your RAM.

A → D → B → F → C

What happens when you traverse a linked list?

  1. Access Node A → 🔴 Cache Miss (CPU fetches from slow RAM)
  2. Go to Node D (stored far away) → 🔴 Cache Miss
  3. Go to Node B (stored elsewhere) → 🔴 Cache Miss

Because the nodes aren’t next to each other, the 64-byte cache line the CPU loaded is useless. The CPU has to constantly go back to the RAM for every single step.

The Takeaway

Big-O tells you how an algorithm scales. Hardware tells you how fast it actually runs.

For most real-world workloads — especially tight loops over collections — arrays (or array-backed structures like std::vector, slice in Go, ArrayList in Java) will outperform linked lists, even when textbook complexity says otherwise.

Always remember: your code runs on a machine, not on a chalkboard. ⚡
entry.summary: Big-O says array access is O(1) and linked-list access is O(n). But the real-world speed difference comes from somewhere else entirely — the CPU cache.

entry.title: The $10,000 Typo: Why You Should Automate Your Local Workflow

link.title: The $10,000 Typo: Why You Should Automate Your Local Workflow

entry.content:
🚨 Imagine this…

It’s 4:55 PM on a Friday.

You’ve been debugging a stubborn API integration all day. Finally, it works!

You quickly run:

git commit -m "fixed integration"
git push

You shut your laptop and head into the weekend 😌

⏳ One day later…

Your phone starts blowing up.

In your rush, you accidentally:

  • Hardcoded a production AWS Access Key
  • Pushed it to a repository

Bots are already scanning GitHub in seconds. By the time you notice, attackers may have already spun up resources costing real money.

Even in private repositories, secrets should never be hardcoded or pushed into Git. Multiple developers still access the same codebase.

Code should never contain secrets — only reference them securely.

💥 Human error is inevitable. And relying on memory alone is risky.

🧠 So how do we stop the “Friday evening disaster”?

👉 We use a pre-commit hook.

✅ Solving the Problem Using Automation

By setting up a pre-commit hook, we tell Git:

“Before you allow this commit to be created, run a script to scan the staged files. If the script finds an API key, reject the commit and throw an error.”

This shifts security to the very beginning of the process. The insecure code never leaves your local machine. It catches the mistake before the pipeline fails, before the code is reviewed, and before a leak occurs.

🪝 What Are Git Hooks?

Git hooks are a built-in feature of Git that serve as the ultimate defense mechanism against human error.

Simply put, they are custom scripts that automatically run whenever a specific Git event occurs — such as before you commit (pre-commit), before you push (pre-push), or after you merge.

Every Git repository already has them! If you look inside the hidden .git/hooks folder, you’ll find sample scripts waiting to be activated.

💻 The Secret Scanner

Here is how simple it is to protect yourself. Create a custom script inside your .git/hooks/pre-commit file:

🧠 Git Hook: Pre-commit Protection

#!/bin/sh

# Check staged files for sensitive keywords
if git diff --cached | grep -qE "API_KEY|console\.log"; then
  echo "🚨 ERROR: Commit rejected!"
  echo "You left an API_KEY or console.log in your code."

  exit 1
fi

exit 0

Now, Git will forcefully stop any commit containing sensitive data, saving you from a massive headache.

That’s only an example; there are many more use cases of Git hooks. Try to figure it out and apply it in your work.
entry.summary: A single careless commit on a Friday evening can cost thousands. Here is how a tiny pre-commit hook can save you from the disaster.
